title: Longest Unequal Adjacent Groups Subsequence II
statement:
You get two arrays of the same length `n`: `words`, whose strings are all different (and may have different lengths), and the integer array `groups`. Pick indices `i_0 < i_1 < ... < i_(k-1)` from `0` to `n - 1` so that every two consecutive picks `a` and `b` obey both rules:

- `groups[a]` and `groups[b]` are not equal;
- `words[a]` and `words[b]` have the same length and differ at exactly one position (their Hamming distance, the count of positions holding different characters, is 1).

Make `k` as large as possible and return the picked words in index order. If several longest choices exist, any one of them is accepted.
constraints: All strings in words are distinct
words[i] contains only lowercase English letters
notes:
## Intuition

Trying every subsequence works for a handful of words but grows as 2^n. Notice that whether a word may follow another depends only on that pair, so this is a longest-increasing-subsequence shape: for each index, ask how long the best valid chain ending exactly there can be. A chain ending at `i` is a chain ending at some earlier compatible `j`, plus `i` itself. Remember which `j` gave the best length and the chain can be rebuilt backwards.

## Approach

1. `dp[i]` is the length of the longest valid chain ending at index `i` (at least 1, the word alone); `prev[i]` is the index before `i` in that chain, or -1.
2. For each `i`, look at every earlier `j`. Skip it when the groups match or when it cannot improve `dp[i]`.
3. Otherwise, if `words[j]` and `words[i]` have equal length and exactly one differing position (`oneApart`), set `dp[i] = dp[j] + 1` and `prev[i] = j`.
4. Track `bestEnd`, the index with the largest `dp`.
5. Follow `prev` from `bestEnd` back to -1, collecting words, and reverse them.

## Example 1, step by step

`words = ["bab", "dab", "cab"]`, `groups = [1, 2, 2]`. Index 0 starts a chain of 1. Index 1 (`"dab"`): index 0 has another group and differs only in the first letter, so `dp[1] = 2`, `prev[1] = 0`, and `bestEnd = 1`. Index 2 (`"cab"`): index 0 also gives `dp[2] = 2`; index 1 shares group 2 and is skipped. `dp[2]` does not beat `dp[1]`, so the walk back from 1 gives `["bab", "dab"]`. LeetCode shows `["bab", "cab"]`; both have the longest length 2, so both are accepted.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n² · L) with L ≤ 10 the word length: each pair is compared once, letter by letter.
- Space: O(n) for `dp` and `prev`.

## Pitfalls

- Words of different lengths are never neighbours; check the lengths before counting differences.
- The rules apply only to consecutive picks, so two picks further apart may share a group.
- Rebuilding needs `prev`; storing only lengths tells you how long the answer is, not which words form it.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `dp[i]` | length of the longest valid chain ending at `i` |
| `prev[i]` | index before `i` in that chain, or -1 |
| `bestEnd` | index where the longest chain ends |
| `oneApart` | true when two words have equal length and differ in one letter |
| `diff` | count of differing letters inside `oneApart` |
| `result` | the words collected while walking back |
